Mist packed so tight between the trunks it reads nearly white; the wet flowers right in front of it look scissored out of paper, every petal edge impossibly sharp against that bright mass.
The mist is pouring sideways through the gap between two trunks fast enough to watch — one strand of hanging moss bent hard to the left by it, the second trunk behind already dissolving.
A clean shaft of angled light cuts down through the mist and the mist itself glows all along the shaft — the wet air is the lit thing, solid-looking, the trunks on either side left dark.
The second trunk back has gone soft grey; the third is a paler rumour of bark; the fourth is simply the same white nothing the mist is made of. The near limb is razor.
Mist thinning for just a moment — a whole dripping wall of fern and green bark appears behind the near limb, fully formed, then the white presses back in and takes it.
The underside of the mist is pressing down between the trunks so hard the air below it sits clear and very dark, and the air above it is a solid white ceiling going nowhere.
Rain starting heavy — the whole mist lights up pale all at once, every leaf in front of it pinging with drops, the moss on the near bark suddenly beading fast and running.
Mist lit hard from behind: every hanging strand of moss in the foreground goes black against the bright mass, thin black lines on white, the trunk behind them already gone.
A hole torn in the mist shows more forest on the other side — another wet trunk, another curtain of moss — and the edges of the hole are already curling inward, the gap closing.
The mist snagged on the ragged top of a tree fern and shredding there, pulling apart in slow torn strands while the trunk below the fern stays sharp and the air around it churns.
Mist standing dead still. Not one strand of moss moves. The second trunk sits in it like something preserved, the third trunk sits in it like something almost gone.
The mist stands so high between the trunks that only one trunk-top on the left still breaks clear of it, its wet bark dark, its top running out of frame into more wet green above.
The mist so full of water it is visibly beading out onto the moss of the nearest trunk — each grey-green lobe of moss is tipped with a bead — the air behind them visibly thick.
Mist that has gone gold in one wide strip across the middle of the frame and stayed slate-grey everywhere else; the trunks crossing through the gold strip are briefly amber.
Mist rising up off the slope from below and streaming upward past the near limb — the motion is all vertical, the moss on the underside of the limb lifting slightly in the current.
Mist so thin here it is barely a gauze, but still the far trunk reads soft and the near bark reads hard — the gauze is doing its work, degrees of gone in a single frame.
Two trunks close together on the left, mist packing in behind them and between them, so what should be the gap between the trunks is also white, the gap solid, the solid mist-shaped.
The mist is moving to the right — one whole bank of it sliding past slowly — and the second trunk behind the near one appears, then is covered again, then appears.

The mist behind the near limb is packed so solid that it is the only thing back there, a soft bright wall of wet air, and the limb runs across the full width of the frame with that wall pressed right up against it.
Mist low between the trunks with clear dark air above it up to the canopy — every hanging root above the mist line is sharp against the dark; every trunk below vanishes into white.
A ragged tendril of mist has found the gap between two limbs and is thickening there, packing itself into the space the light was using, the limbs above and below both still sharp.
The mist is thin enough to backlight but too thick to see through — every dripping root in front of it is a dark stroke, and behind them the white is even and deep and going nowhere.
Two separate layers of mist, one close — soft — one further — barely a stain of grey — and between them a brief slot of wet green that both layers are already reaching toward.
Mist so thick the near trunk seems to be floating, its lower half dissolved into the white, only the mossy upper bark still reading as bark, the rest of the frame white in all directions.
The mist pressing in from the right side of the frame only — left side clear enough to show bark texture — right side nothing — the mist's own edge a slow soft vertical line crossing the picture.
